title: An Indian Diplomat Was Found Dead Inside the Mission in Bangladesh. New Delhi Isn’t Saying a Word.
excerpt: Naren Dhar, an assistant protocol officer at the Indian High Commission in Chattogram, was discovered lifeless on a Tuesday morning. The silence from both governments is deafening.
body:
The body of Naren Dhar was found on the second floor of the old visa centre building at India’s Assistant High Commission in Chattogram, Bangladesh, on Tuesday morning. He was in front of a bathroom door. He was in his late 30s. He was from Chandigarh.

That is nearly everything that is publicly known.

Dhar served as an assistant protocol officer at the mission — a mid-level posting at one of India’s most sensitive diplomatic outposts in a country where bilateral relations have been strained for months. Local police, who reached the scene after being informed of the incident, sent his body for autopsy at the Chattogram Medical College Hospital.

“We have been told he was Naren Dhar and serving as the assistant protocol officer at the mission,” Aminur Rashid, the port city’s assistant police commissioner, told reporters.

No injury marks were found on the body, according to police. The initial suspicion is cardiac arrest, but as Inspector Nazrul Islam of Khulshi Police Station noted: “The exact cause of death cannot be determined without an autopsy.”

## A Wall of Silence

What makes the case unusual is not the death itself — sudden cardiac events claim young professionals with grim regularity — but the institutional silence that followed.

The Indian High Commission in Dhaka has not commented. The Assistant High Commission in Chattogram has not commented. India’s Ministry of External Affairs has not issued a statement. The Bangladeshi government has been equally quiet.

Chattogram Metropolitan Police deputy commissioner Amirul Islam confirmed that an unnatural death case would be filed, a standard procedure when a foreign national dies on diplomatic premises. Dhar’s remains will be handed over to Indian mission officials after the post-mortem.

But for the families of Indian diplomats posted abroad — and for the broader diplomatic community watching from New Delhi — the silence raises more questions than it answers.

## The India-Bangladesh Backdrop

The death comes at a fraught moment in India-Bangladesh relations. Since the political upheaval in Dhaka that saw Sheikh Hasina’s ouster, the bilateral relationship has deteriorated sharply. India has flagged over 2,800 verification requests after Dhaka warned against “push-backs” of undocumented migrants. New Delhi recently appointed former Trinamool Congress leader Dinesh Trivedi as its new high commissioner to Bangladesh — a move seen as an attempt to reset ties through political signalling rather than career diplomacy.

Chattogram itself is strategically significant. The port city is Bangladesh’s commercial capital and a critical node in regional trade routes. India’s consular presence there handles visa processing, trade facilitation, and the welfare of Indian nationals — functions that have become more sensitive as cross-border tensions simmer.

Against this backdrop, the death of even a mid-level officer inside a diplomatic compound carries weight. While there is no evidence linking Dhar’s death to anything beyond a medical emergency, the diplomatic context makes the official silence more conspicuous.

## What the Diaspora Needs to Know

For NRIs, the incident is a reminder of the human cost behind the abstraction of “bilateral relations.” Indian diplomatic staff posted to difficult missions — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, conflict zones in the Middle East — often work under intense pressure with limited support infrastructure. Mid-level officers like Dhar, who handle the unglamorous daily operations of consular work, rarely make headlines until something goes wrong.

The lack of any public acknowledgement from New Delhi is itself notable. When Indian diplomats have faced incidents abroad — the 2013 arrest of diplomat Devyani Khobragade in New York, the 2019 harassment of Indian officials in Pakistan — the government has typically responded swiftly and publicly. The silence around Dhar’s death suggests either a deliberate decision to avoid inflaming an already delicate diplomatic situation, or an investigation that has not yet reached conclusions the government is willing to share.

## What Happens Next

An autopsy will determine the cause of death. If it confirms a natural cause, the incident will likely recede from public attention. If it doesn’t, the case could become another pressure point in a relationship that can ill afford one.

For now, Naren Dhar’s family in Chandigarh waits. The diplomatic machinery grinds on. And a 38-year-old man who went to work at an Indian mission in Bangladesh did not come home.
author: Diaspora Desk
